z-m-39-01.title: Can different values have the same sum?
z-m-39-01.topic: The meaning of a function and one-to-one functions: a sum condition on the values and the size of the codomain
z-m-39-01.goal: Use a counterexample to confirm that the meaning of a one-to-one function (different elements correspond to different values) says nothing about the sums of the values, and explain that whether a function with the same condition exists depends on the codomain.
z-m-39-01.material: Think of a function f from the domain X={1, 2, 3, 4} to the codomain Y={1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} as a table of values. The table lists only f(1), f(2), f(3), f(4) (there is no formula). Condition (가): f is a one-to-one function, that is, different elements of X correspond to different values. Condition (나): f(1)+f(4)=f(2)+f(3). Mina said, “If it's one-to-one, all four values are different. Then the sums of two pairs can't be equal like in (나).”
z-m-39-01.thinking.0: Moving the claim into a table of values and testing it
z-m-39-01.thinking.1: Building different examples (counterexamples) that satisfy the conditions
z-m-39-01.thinking.2: Judging conditionally whether such a function exists when the codomain changes
z-m-39-01.prereq.0: The meaning of function, domain, codomain, and range, and the meaning of a one-to-one function (the first part of the functions unit of high school common mathematics)
z-m-39-01.prereq.1: Counting the elements of a set
z-m-39-01.prereq.2: (School-sequence assumption: the H2 of this task is only a difficulty label assigned in production, and we assume the prerequisites above have already been learned.)
z-m-39-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose your first judgment of Mina's statement. (You don't have to calculate yet.)
z-m-39-01.s.s1.hint.0: Think of f(1), f(2), f(3), f(4) as four blanks, and fill in four different numbers.
z-m-39-01.s.s1.hint.1: With the numbers you filled in, write f(1)+f(4) and f(2)+f(3) separately and compare whether they are equal.
z-m-39-01.s.s1.o.a: Right. If all four values are different, the sums of the two pairs are also different
z-m-39-01.s.s1.r.a: You are treating “the values are different” and “the sums are different” as the same statement. Pick two different pairs of numbers yourself and compare the sums.
z-m-39-01.s.s1.o.b: Right. A one-to-one function gets larger as x gets larger, so the sums cannot be equal
z-m-39-01.s.s1.r.b: You are treating a one-to-one function and an increasing function as the same. Think about whether there are one-to-one functions whose values decrease.
z-m-39-01.s.s1.o.c: Wrong. Even if all the values are different, the sums of two different pairs can be equal
z-m-39-01.s.s1.r.c: You read the claim as “always” and doubted whether an example exists. Now it is time to test whether such an example can really be built.
z-m-39-01.s.s1.o.d: We can't judge. It's because the formula of f is not given
z-m-39-01.s.s1.r.d: You are thinking of a function only as a formula. Here, the table of four values alone is enough to test the conditions.
z-m-39-01.s.s1.explain: The condition of being a one-to-one function says only that the four values are different. Whether the sums of two pairs can be equal even when the four values are different has to be checked by actually finding an example. Let's test it in the next step.
z-m-39-01.s.s2.prompt: Using a table of values, build 2 functions f that satisfy both conditions (가) and (나) and have f(1) greater than f(2). The two functions must use different sets of values. (a=f(1), b=f(2), c=f(3), d=f(4); all integers from 1 to 7)
z-m-39-01.s.s2.hint.0: First find a group of four different numbers for which f(1)+f(4) and f(2)+f(3) are equal.
z-m-39-01.s.s2.hint.1: Place the four numbers you found so that f(1) is greater than f(2), and check again that the two sums are still equal.
z-m-39-01.s.s2.hint.2: Find one more group whose numbers themselves are different from those used in the first function.
z-m-39-01.s.s2.ok.c1: All four values are elements of the codomain Y (integers from 1 to 7).
z-m-39-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Every value must be an integer from 1 to 7.
z-m-39-01.s.s2.ok.c2: All four values are different, so it is a one-to-one function.
z-m-39-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The same value was used twice. It is not a one-to-one function.
z-m-39-01.s.s2.fail.c3: f(1)+f(4) and f(2)+f(3) are not equal.
z-m-39-01.s.s2.fail.c4: f(1) is not greater than f(2).
z-m-39-01.s.s2.explain: For example, (3, 1, 6, 4) has 3+4=7=1+6 and all four values are different. So Mina's claim does not hold. Also, since there is an example with f(1)>f(2), a one-to-one function does not only map toward larger values. ((1, 2, 3, 4) satisfies the sum condition but breaks f(1)>f(2), so it is not accepted at this step.)
z-m-39-01.s.s3.prompt: New information: the domain stays X={1, 2, 3, 4} and conditions (가) and (나) stay the same, but the codomain Y is changed as shown below. Choose all the codomains for which a function f satisfying the conditions can be made. (There is no condition f(1)>f(2).)
z-m-39-01.s.s3.hint.0: In each codomain, choose four different numbers, split them into two pairs, and write the sums of the two pairs side by side.
z-m-39-01.s.s3.hint.1: If the codomain has fewer than 4 elements, first count to check whether a one-to-one function can be made at all.
z-m-39-01.s.s3.r.a: It seems you thought that having 5 elements is plenty. Choose four of them, split them into two pairs, and write out for yourself whether there is a case where the sums are equal.
z-m-39-01.s.s3.r.b: You looked not only at the number of elements but also at the fact that the numbers are evenly spaced. Check whether you found two pairs with equal sums.
z-m-39-01.s.s3.r.c: If you look at the sum condition first, it is easy to miss that there are not enough elements. First count how many values are needed to be a one-to-one function.
z-m-39-01.s.s3.r.d: You checked whether a codomain of the same size as the domain also has two pairs with equal sums. You considered the case where all four numbers are used.
z-m-39-01.s.s3.explain: {1,2,3} has only 3 elements, so the four elements of X cannot have different values, and there is no one-to-one function at all. {1,2,3,4} has 1+4=2+3, and {2,5,8,11,14} has two pairs with equal sums such as 2+14=5+11. {1,2,4,8,16} has 5 elements, but there is no case where the sums of two different pairs are equal. It is not that having many elements is enough; which numbers they are is what matters.
z-m-39-01.s.s4.prompt: Explain to Mina. Write (1) where the original claim is wrong, with a numerical example, and (2) that a function with the same conditions does not always exist, using a codomain.
z-m-39-01.s.s4.hint.0: Take one of the tables you made in step 2 as it is, and write the four values and the two sums.
z-m-39-01.s.s4.hint.1: Choose one codomain you did not choose in step 3, and write in one sentence why a function could not be made with that codomain.
z-m-39-01.s.s4.placeholder: Example: A one-to-one function means ..., but ...
z-m-39-01.s.s4.selfAssess.0: In your numerical example, is it clear that the four values are all different and the sums of the two pairs are equal?
z-m-39-01.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you separate what “one-to-one” tells us from what it does not tell us?
z-m-39-01.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Did you give examples (a case with too few elements, or a case with no pairs of equal sums) showing that depending on the codomain a function may or may not exist?
z-m-39-01.s.s4.model.0: Four different values can still have equal sums. For example, if f(1)=3, f(2)=1, f(3)=6, f(4)=4, then the values are all different and 3+4=1+6=7. But if the codomain is a set like {1, 2, 4, 8, 16}, which has no two pairs with equal sums, such a function can't be made.
z-m-39-01.s.s4.model.1: A one-to-one function only means the values don't overlap; it doesn't mean the sums are different. If f(1)=2, f(2)=1, f(3)=4, f(4)=3, then 2+3=1+4=5, so the sums are equal. But if the codomain has only 3 elements, there isn't even a one-to-one function, so depending on what set the codomain is, a function may or may not exist.
z-m-39-01.s.s4.modelNote.1: It did not mention whether the values are increasing, but it has both the counterexample and the codomain condition.
